summary: This work demonstrates an analog-digital hybrid quantum simulator using $^{87}$Rb Rydberg atom arrays, coherently mapping between interacting Rydberg and digital hyperfine qubits to engineer and probe complex many-body dynamics. On a 271-site kagome lattice, the team prepares a non-equilibrium $\mathrm{U}(1)$ quantum spin liquid via Floquet driving and closed-loop optimization, observing key signatures including equal-amplitude dimer superpositions, many-body coherences extending over 18 sites, and universal correlations matching field theory predictions.
motivation: Understanding out-of-equilibrium quantum criticality and exotic phases like quantum spin liquids is challenging because they are difficult to prepare in equilibrium and conventionally require large-depth digital circuits. The authors sought to overcome these limitations by combining efficient analog evolution with programmable digital control and error detection.
method: Coherent mapping between hyperfine and Rydberg qubits enables arbitrary state preparation and measurement while using non-destructive readout for loss detection and qubit reuse. The team engineered effective Hamiltonians via Floquet driving—demonstrating six-body ring exchange and two-body hopping on 1D chains—and optimized a detuning sweep protocol using Bayesian optimization to target the Rokhsar-Kivelson point on the honeycomb quantum dimer model.
result: On the kagome lattice, the optimized 0.8 μs sweep prepared a state with mean Rydberg density approaching $1/3$ filling, projected kinetic and potential energies both $\approx 0.29$ (close to RK prediction), uniform distribution over dimer configurations, X-loop coherences persisting over 33 sites (decaying as perimeter law), and rectified dimer-dimer and dimer-string correlators with a ratio of $4$ as predicted by the emergent $\mathrm{U}(1)$ gauge theory.
